newsitem.title: FRANCE: French defence minister to visit Israel next week.
newsitem.headline: French defence minister to visit Israel next week.

text.p: French Defence Minister Charles Millon will visit Israel next week in a new sign of warming relations between the two countries.
His spokesman Pierre Servent told reporters on Thursday that Millon would leave on February 11 and return on the night of February 13-14.
"The visit will take place in the framework of the renewal of bilateral relations which began in 1993," he said.
Franco-Israeli ties were cool after Paris slapped an arms embargo on Israel following the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.

Millon will meet President Ezer Weizman, Foreign Minister David Levy and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai. A meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will depend on whether the Israeli leader is in the country at the time, Servent said.
The schedule includes "a private visit" to Jerusalem about which Servent gave no details except that Millon would not go to the Palestinian Authority's Orient House office in Arab East Jerusalem.
Israeli officials have clashed with foreign countries over visits by envoys to Orient House as they say East Jerusalem is part of Israel .

Millon's visit is one of several French ministerial visits recently announced by Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who is seeking to mend bridges with French Jews ahead of France's 1998 general election and after a controversial Middle East tour by President Jacques Chirac in October, criticised as biased in favour of the Arab states.

France, which wants to keep good relations with rich Arab states and continued access to their markets, is traditionally secretive about the exact nature of its ties with Israel which were re-initiated four years ago by then defence minister Francois Leotard.
France, which once single-handedly equipped the Israeli Air Force, recently purchased Israeli unmanned drone reconnaissance aircraft.

Unspecified scientific cooperation is known to exist in military domains as well as exchanges between intelligence services equally worried by Islamic fundamentalist guerrillas who have struck in both countries.
